policy_title: Increase Universal Credit, benefits, and pensions
stated: Increase Universal Credit and legacy benefits by £40 a week, end the five-week waiting period, abolish the two-child benefit cap, increase all disability benefits by 5%, uprate pensions with inflation and wage rises, and increase carer’s allowance by at least 10% a month. Scrap the bedroom tax.

source.quote: Elected Greens will campaign to: • Increase Universal Credit and legacy benefits by £40 a week. • End the unfair five-week wait for benefits which is pushing people into debt. • Abolish the two-child benefit cap and lift 250,000 children out of poverty. • Increase all disability benefits by 5%. • Ensure that pensions are always uprated in line with inflation and keep pace with wage rises across the economy. • Increase carer’s allowance by at least 10% a month. • Scrap the bedroom tax.

bearing_set.reason: A £40/week UC uplift, ending the 5-week wait, abolishing the two-child cap, and raising disability/carer's benefits directly and materially increases disposable income for low-income households — the core cost-of-living indicator.
Uprating pensions with both inflation and wage rises directly affects the real value of the state pension and pensioner poverty — a core O8 indicator.

Scrapping the bedroom tax (spare room subsidy) directly reduces Housing Benefit deductions for social tenants deemed to under-occupy, affecting their ability to afford and remain in their homes — a genuine housing-affordability effect for that tenure group.

The entire package is concentrated on lower-income households (UC claimants, disabled people, carers, large families), mechanically narrowing the income gap and improving the Gini/bottom-quintile indicator.

A £40/week UC increase alone would cost tens of billions annually; combined with pension, disability and carer's uplifts this is a very large spending commitment that, if unfunded, materially widens the structural deficit and worsens debt-path sustainability.

membership_note: Five fundamentals are warranted because this is a bundled multi-measure policy spanning working-age benefits, disability support, pensions, carer's payments and housing benefit — each sub-measure maps to a distinct indicator. The dominant effects are improved living standards for lower-income groups (O2, O14), pensioner security (O8), housing cost relief (O1), and a fiscal cost that bears squarely on O12.
